title: Imports and Exports
objective: After this level you can explain imports, exports and the balance of trade.
summary: Exports are sold abroad and imports are bought from abroad; travel spending counts too. Exports minus imports gives the trade balance, and whether a deficit matters is debated.

cards.headline: Buy a souvenir on holiday abroad, and your country just imported something.
cards.body: No ship, no container, no customs form. Yet the statisticians count it. What foreign visitors spend in a country counts as its exports, and what its residents spend on trips abroad counts as imports.

cards.headline: Out the door, in the door
cards.body: An export is a good or service a country sells to other countries; an import is one it buys from them. Exports bring money in, and imports send it out. Goods like cars and coffee count, but so do services: finance, software, consulting and design. So does your holiday. A tourist eating pasta in Rome is, technically, an Italian export.

mascot.line: Next time someone asks about your trip, tell them you were supporting Italian exports.

cards.headline: Keeping score
cards.body: Take exports, subtract imports, and you get the trade balance. Export more than you import and you run a trade surplus. Import more and you run a trade deficit. The United States has run a deficit year after year since the mid-1970s. So is it losing?

cards.fact: Is a trade deficit a loss? People disagree.
cards.context: Some policymakers see a deficit as proof that a country is losing at trade. Most experts say a deficit, or a surplus, is in itself neither good nor bad. Remember Level 71: each trade happens because both sides expect to gain. Whether a country's overall deficit is a problem is a separate, and still debated, question.

cards.headline: Imports, exports, balance
learned: Exports are sold abroad; imports are bought from abroad

questions.prompt: A tourist from Japan pays for a museum ticket in New York. For the US, what is that spending?

options.label: An import of services
options.rationale: It would be an import for Japan, not the US.

options.label: Not trade at all
options.rationale: Services, including travel, count as trade.

options.label: A tariff
options.rationale: A tariff is a tax on imports, not a purchase.

questions.explanation: What foreign visitors spend in a country counts as that country's exports, so the ticket is a US export.

questions.prompt: A country exports $50 billion and imports $70 billion in a year. What does it have?

options.label: A trade surplus of $20 billion
options.rationale: A surplus needs exports bigger than imports.

options.label: A trade surplus of $120 billion
options.rationale: The balance subtracts imports from exports; it doesn't add them.

options.label: A balanced trade account
options.rationale: It imports more than it exports, so it isn't balanced.

questions.explanation: Exports minus imports is 50 minus 70, or minus 20: a trade deficit of $20 billion.

questions.prompt: Level 71 said voluntary trades make both sides better off. What do most experts say about a trade deficit in itself?

options.label: It proves a country is losing
options.rationale: That's the view of some policymakers, not most experts.

options.label: It is neither good nor bad
It is always a sign of strength
options.rationale: Experts don't call it a sign of strength either.

options.label: It means trade has stopped
options.rationale: A deficit means imports exceed exports; trade continues.

questions.explanation: Most experts say a deficit or surplus is in itself neither good nor bad, though some policymakers see deficits as losing.
